House in committee on Bill (No. 20) to prevent the introduction or speading of insects, pests and diseases destructive to vegetation.-Mr. Fisher.

The object of this Bill, as I gather, is to give the Minister of Agriculture greater power to deal with insects and all pests and diseases destructive to vegetation. The Bill, 'by section 10, repeals the San Jose Scale Act of 1898. This Bill gives very much larger powers, is wider in its scope and it is possible that in the exercise of those powers there may be some clash with the provincial jurisdiction. I would, therefore, like rapidly to run over the considerations that one is anxious to put forward with regard to a measure of this kind. About the year 1895 the San Jose scale was first discovered on this continent, or rather in the eastern part of the continent, by Professor Howard, of Washington, and those of us who are interested in commercial horticulture are aware how rapidly this particular insect spread all over the United States and Canada. It was about 1897 or 1898 that the first case was discovered in Canada, not very far from where I lived in the province of Ontario. The second case happened to come under my personal notice about four miles from St. Catharines and it proved that this insect had become established in Ontario. After some discussion, which I do not want to go into now, and after all the information that Professor Howard and other authorities could give with regard to the danger involved in the establishment of an insect of this kind, the government introduced what was called the San Jose Scale Act of 1898. There have been some steps taken to try and control this insect pest by the provincial government of Ontario, and very vigorous measures were adopted which have cost the government of Ontario a great many thousands of dollars since. But the Bill introduced by the government in 1898 dealt

only with this one insect, the San Jose scale, and the operations of the Bill were directed against it in only one way, that is to say, by the inspection of importations of nursery stock at certain points of entry designated by the minister. Therefore, as far as federal powers go. the only method under which they dealt with inspection or with any comprehensive system of inspection with regard to insect pests and diseases was that which I have outlined. This Bill, now before the committee, gives power to inspect and deal with all insects, pests and diseases destructive to vegetation, and it gives wide powers which, if exercised indiscriminately, may perhaps lead to unfortunate results. We have these powers given in sections 5, 6, 7 and 8. The minister may appoint inspectors and other persons to perform this work and may exercise certain other powers which are set out clearly in these four clauses. The minister, under this Bill, would have ample power to deal in a very comprehensive way with this _ matter in any province in the Dominion. I may add that I am aware that the jurisdiction is concurrent, that is to say that while the various provinces have power to deal with all these things, apparently the power lies also equally with the Dominion authorities. Of course, the minister will understand that I am not speaking in any spirit of hostility with reference to Dominion regulations or to the powers given under this or any other Bill, but I just want to make clear to the minister and to the committee what the position is in British Columbia in regard to these various matters. The minister himself is familiar with many of the conditions there. In British Columbia 21 years ago we established what is known as the Board of Horticulture. There was a special Act passed for that purpose and that Board of Horticulture was composed of three members representing the various portions of the province and also having as members the Minister of Agriculture and the deputy minister of agriculture. We have two statutory meetings a year, but during, last year we held about five meetings. The members act in an advisory capacity to the government, that is they advise them on every kind ot question and every piece of legislation with regard to horticultural matters. They formulate and alter regulations from time to time in the best interests of the horticultural industry. We have also established under the authority of the Act and under the authority of the board, fumigation stations, a central inspection office with a chief inspector and something like thirty sub-inspectors. I have been a member of that board for something like four years and I am fairly familiar with its operations and what was aimed at in its Mr. BURRELL.
creation. We have been so careful and so rigid in our methods and in our control of the fruit industry under this Act and under this board that I think I am safe in saying that it has resulted in a cleanliness in our orchards and fruit production that places them second to none on the whole continent. We have followed the practice of systematically inspecting, examining and fumigating nursery stock from any part of the world or from eastern Canada, because, although it is true that the Dominion government has fumigating stations we do not take that as a sufficient safeguard of our own horticultural interests. Then, we also	have a thorough
system of inspecting every tree that comes in because the tree itself may be a medium of danger and infection either by fungus or insect pest. We, also, examine all the fruit which comes in from the Orient, the United States, Australasia, Eastern Canada, or any other point. We met with a great deal of opposition from the wholesale importers of fruit in the establishment of a thorough system of inspection, and that opposition was so strong at times as to be unpleasant. It is not uninteresting to our eastern friends to know that the result of our efforts has been the importation of a better class of fruit than formerly; the growers are not exposed to the same danger of infection, the dealers have been benefited by handling a superior class of fruit, and the consumers get a better quality. The horticultural Board Act has been recently amended so as to increase the membership of the board in recognition of the continually increasing development of the industry in our province. We have appointed several trained inspectors, entomologists and hortieulturalists who have been trained in the eastern colleges, and in this way we have -strengthened very much the machinery with which we are working. As a result of all this, the status of the British Columbia fruit industry is now so high that I do not believe there is another fruit area of equal extent-we have 100,000 acres now under orchard-in America or in the world that is so free from the leading fungus or insect pests. The Minister -of Agriculture has been through our province, and he has had excellent opportunities for seeing our virtues, and perhaps our faults.
I may say that it is a matter of very much regret to us that the minister was not able . to visit one or two of our prominent -districts, such as Kelowna, -of -which he only got a cursory glimpse, for reasons which he himself understands. I regret that all the more, because at Kelowna we have a large acreage under tobacco, and a very interesting tobacco industry there. I think the minister will admit, from his experience in British Columbia, that every word I have said is true, and that we are producing a

remarkably fine commercial product which will hold its own in any market in the world. By the way, there is one little touch I would like to give to the Minister of Agriculture, and I do not think it will do any harm. I quote from a horticultural magazine which has been recently established, the following excerpt from a leading article :
The ' Star ' of December 11, in its report of a meeting of the Pomological and Fruit Growing Society of the province of Quebec, held in the Macdonald College on the 10th ultimo, quotes the Hon. Sydney Fisher as saying that 'the prairies offered a great market for apples, and British Columbia was recognizing this. But the flavour of the British Columbia apple was not to be compared with that of the province of Quebec.'
Of course it is just possible that the Minister of Agriculture regards the British Col umbia apple as so much superior to that of Quebec that it is not to be considered in the same class. But considering that it was a Quebec audience to whom the minister was speaking and that he referred to British Columbia in the negative sense we are forced to conclude that Mr. Fisher, if correctly reported, intended his audience to understand that in his opinion the British Columbia apple was very inferior to that of Quebec.
If one of Mr. Fisher's subordinates were to commit an indiscretion like that he would not only be promptly called to account by the press of the country who knew better, but in all probability he would be severely reprimanded for a breach of etiquette by the minister himself.
Of course, we have to make allowances for the Minister of Agriculture giving an ex parte utterance to an audience in his own province, but as a British Columbian, he cannot expect me to assent to any such heretical doctrine as he lays down there. As a matter of fact, the questions as to the superiority of fruit are in a sense rather dependent upon local conditions in every province, and these local conditions make enormous differences. I venture to think that I could go into one province and take certain samples of fruit and say they were superior to anything produced in another province, and similarly in another province, I could find the result reversed. This, of course, depends altogether on the conditions under which the fruit was grown. I am very certain, however, that the Minister of Agriculture had no ground for making such a sweeping statement as is attributed to him here.
Did he say anything about the Ontario apple?

That was probably too delicate a question for him to touch. I would like to call the attention of the minister, and of the committee, to what we have done in British Columbia in the matter of inspection and. fumigation, because it will be of interest to the country as a
whole. Under the provincial methods of inspection, from January until May of last year we inspected 660,000 seedlings and grafts, and 250,000 standard trees, and a large amount of mixed nursery stock. Out of this amount we condemned-and the committee will understand that except those which came from eastern Ontario, all were fumigated in the Dominion station- we condemned 12,500 standard fruit trees.
What were they condemned for?
I have not the information here to answer that. No doubt some of them would be condemned because of fungus and insect diseases.
It is only fair to say that the Dominion fumigation station only fumigates for the San Jose scale and does not pretend in any way to deal with any other disease.

I quite understand that, but there is a general feeling that the strength of the fumigation required for the San Jose scale would practically insure safety against all other insects except perhaps the brown-tailed moth.

Unless the hon. gentleman can show that his organization found San Jose scale on the plants that went through the Dominion fumigation station, it is not fair to cast any reflection on the work of that station.

I will touch on that point in a moment. From the month of January to October we inspected 96,600 boxes of fruit and condemned 12,200 boxes, and in addition to that, we have also carried the work of inspection to rice, for the weevil, and out of 163,000 sacks of rice we fumigated 14,500. I hope the minister will understand that I am not particularly reflecting on the work of the Dominion fumigation station, except that I would point out that for other reasons (unless a change has been made within the last year) that station has never been satisfactory. To my mind, and to the mind of a great many of our leading fruit growers, the Dominion fumigating station has not been quite up to the mark in the past. We do not want to run any risks in the province of British Columbia, and when we established our fumigating station, we took care to get all the latest methods and improvements to effectually meet the evil, not only in regard to the actual fumigation itself, but also in regard to packing and unpacking, drying out, subjection to frosts, and things of that kind. The actual fumigating room in the Dominion station is 8 by 8, 16 by 8 by 6 by 4 high, and as I think the minister knows, a great part of the platform where the stock is unloaded from the railway cars is exposed and open, and there is

comparatively little room to move along it. The consequence is that only a small quantity can be fumigated at a time in a chamber of that kind. The stock has to be put on the floor, generally in bundles, and fairly tightly packed, and it is pretty hard for the gas to penetrate, in a thoroughly effective wav, all the nursery stock under these conditions. Then there is the further disadvantage of the stock being exposed to drying out, and the difficulty of handling it. The minister apparently did not want to trust us entirely with the duty of fumigating, probably he saw difficulties in the way. However, when we put up our fumigation station we consulted Dr. Willis Johnson the state entomologist of New Jersey. The fumigation station has four rooms. The actual fumigation room was 11 feet by 16 feet by 18 feet. The stock is put on racks, where the fumes penetrate it very freely. The rooms are all air-proof and frost-proof. So that we have a good many advantages in that way. I do not say whether or not we discovered the San Jose scale alive after the stock passed through the Dominion fumigating room, though I think we did. However, we did discover the borers, the aphis and other pests; so that we have had to make a very thorough and systematic inspection of the stock after it nassed the Dominion fumigation station. I do not want to delay the discussion of the Bill now, as it will be taken up later clause by clause. I simply say that we have all this elaborate provincial machinery, and we hope for development on sound lines of our valuable and increasingly valuable fruit industry. 1 have endeavoured to get into as close touch as possible with the leading men connected with the fruit industry in the province, and there is a strong feeling among them that although the jurisdiction is concurrent, we should be very loath to relinquish any of our organization or our methods or our efforts, and we hope that under this Bill, which gives the minister much larger and wider powers, there will not be any clash between the federal and the provincial authorities. I desire to say here that I recognize that the minister, in bringing forward this Bill, is earnestly desirous of coping with anything injurious to the fruit industry of Canada. I frankly make that admission; but I thought it well at this stage to point out -what our general attitude was, so that the minister might give a full explanation of the modus operandi of this measure in order that we should have a clear understanding of it before it went into actual effect.

I appreciate fully the position which the hon. member takes, and I take no exception whatever to any of his statements. In fact, I rather welcome Mr. BURRELL.
them, because I think that his description of what is' being done in British Columbia is one of the best proofs of the advisability of a Bill of this kind being introduced and made applicable to the whole of Canada. I will not delay the House by any reference to my hon. friend's personal opinions of British Columbia fruit, and that of Quebec; but I do not hesitate here, in the face of my hon. friend and others, to maintain the character and quality of the fruit of the province from which I come. I consider the apples of Quebec, as far as quality and flavour are concerned, to be infinitely superior to anything produced not only in British Columbia, but in the whole world.	,
I cannot allow that.
What about Nova Scotia?

I am not going to make an exception of even Nova Scotia. My hon. friend must not accuse me of having made ad captandum statements to the people of Quebec, because when I was in British Columbia I told the people there that if they obtained great prizes abroad, for their apples, it was only because the fruit of Quebec had not been shown at the same exhibition. I appreciate the quality of the fruit of British Columbia, I recognize the great fruit-growing capabilities of that province, and I congratulate it not only on the quality and beauty of its fruit, but on the fact that in recent years especially the increase in fruit-growing in British Columbia has been enormous, and that its prospects in the near future are still brighter. Under these circumstances I do not hesitate, while standing up for my own province, as far as quality is concerned, to recognize the superior producing character of the great province of British Columbia in regard to actual production. My hon. friend twitted me with not having visited Kelowna. I could not visit every place in the province, and the connections were such that I could not make it convenient to visit Kelowna; but I can assure my hon. friend and the people of Kelowna that I have not forgotten them nor their hospitable intentions, nor their great interest in fruit-growing, and tobacco-growing, and I hope very soon to give an evidence of the value I place on their tobacco-growing work by aiding it in some substantial way. Having disposed of these extraneous matters. let me come to the Bill before the House. I accept my hon. friend's compliment in the spirit in which it is given; but I have introduced this Bill in the interest not only of fruit-growing, but of treegrowing in the Dominion of Canada. Insect pests attack other things than fruit trees and fruit, and it is just as important to protect our forests and shrubbery as our

orchards, and our fruit trees. But I recognize also the good work being done in British Columbia, under the Provincial Act. If as good work were done all over Canada as has been done in British Columbia, under that Act, the necessity for this Bill would be to a large extent removed. I believe that the inspection under the British Columbia Act is as good as any on the continent of America, or perhaps, even better. I have watched it with great interest, and have sympathized with the efforts of the British Columbia people to legislate for the protection of their orchards and forests. I think the work done there has been excellent for the province, and has had excellent results. In that respect my hon. friend and I are absolutely at one.
I would like to remind my hon. friend that when the fumigating station at Vancouver was established, the importations of nursery stock into British Columbia were far less than to-day, and the station was then established on a scale which Dr. Fletcher considered sufficient. I am aware that its capacity and arrangements are today not quite what they might be, and had it not been for my expectation of passing this Bill this session, I would have taken steps last year to re-arrange and improve that station. I thought it possible however, that when this Bill came into force we might have to provide for other work besides fumigating the San Jose scale. In these fumigating station's we have not attempted to more than protect against the introduction of the San Jose scale and for that purpose there is just one kind of fumigation. But in dealing with other pests, we may have to use other methods, because that which might be effective in the one case might not necessarily be in others. I am not sufficiently familiar with the insect pests to say what these are, but it is quite possible that there are other pests which the fumigation would not destroy. It is therefore quite possible that the provincial government inspectors may have found in nursery stock that passed through our fumigating stations in Vancouver other insect pests. My hon. friend seems to think it possible that they have found the San Jose scale. I do not think so. Since the establishment of these stations, not only in British Columbia but in the other provinces, not one case of San Jose scale has been in any way traced to imported stock, and all imported stock goes through our fumigating stations.. Under these circumstances, I am justified in assuming that these stations have been effective and that mw hon. friend's impression is not founded on fact. I can only regret extremely that if, on any occasion, the inspectors of the provincial government found anything of the kind, they did not take trouble to report fio us, so that we might investigate and remedy any deficiency or carelessness which might have oc-cured at any of our stations. We have no report that anything of the kind has oc-cured, no complaint has been made to us, and I think that I am justified in assuming that the impression under which my hon. friend labours is absolutely unfounded.
The provisions of this Bill are very similar in a general way to those of the British Columbia Act which my hon. friend has praised. I did not take that Act particularly as my model although it was thoroughly studied by us. What we took was rather the Act of Great Britain which seemed to suit our purposes here, and we have drafted a Bill which we think will cover the same ground and accomplish the same purposes as the British Act.
The conflict which my hon. friend thinks possible between this parliament and .the provincial legislature I trust will not arise. As far as I am concerned, wherever it can be shown that the provincial authorities are taking all the necessary steps, I shall be very loath to interfere. I am not at all anx'ious for unnecessary w ork, and Jf have no desire to assume any responsibility or labour which does not fall naturally to my lot. If a provincial legislature takes the necessary precautions and carries them out efficiently, as I think the British Columbia people are doing, I shall not interfere with its work or try to overlap or duplicate it. But at the same time I think that an Act of this kind should, in the interests of the whole country, be passed and applied bo the Dominion at large and not merely to one province. Otherwise while British Columbia might be very well safeguarded, the rest of the Dominion might not, and the danger of spreading infection elsewhere is entirely outside the purview of the British Columbia authorities. By means of a general law we can protect the whole Dominion much better than it can be by any number of Provincial Acts. I do not understand that my hon. friend objects at all to the passage of this Bill. I am sure he recognizes that it is quite within the competence of this parliament. That opinion I do not presume to give on my own authority, but I have the assurance of the Department of Justice that this Bill is absolutely within our jurisdiction. British Columbia may have no doubt a similar jurisdiction within the limits of that province, but I understand that by the British North America Act, where jurisdiction is given to both provincial and federal parliaments, and a conflict arises, the federal authority must prevail. I can, however, assure my hon. friend that I shall not undertake to interfere in any way with the provincial work. It would be only when I found it necessary in the interests of the country at large, that anything should be done in any province, that I would take

such steps as this Bill empowers me to take.	.
As the results of our work, done with the concurrence and assistance of the importers, willingly given to us-hut possibly given to us because they anticipated a Bill of this kind and felt that the sacrifices they made this year would be followed up by continuous safety in the future-by reason of that wfOrk, we have been able to inspect 1,700,000,000 seedlings since the first of January, and found 293 nests of the brown tail moth. I have no doubt that each nest contained 200 to 300 caterpillars which would mean some 60,000 caterpillars or more, and if these had gone abroad throughout Canada and had been able to reproduce themselves in the way these insects do. we might easily have had this coming season a very severe and expensive visitation of this pest. That was done by volunteer work with only one official in addition to our regular staff, and I have no doubt we will be able to do our work more efficiently by having it legally recognized.

I have already said I am in favour of this measure, and since the minister has given us to understand it is not going to be interfered with in any way by the provincial governments, we can more readily acquiesce in it. I was sorry to hear the minister say that he has stated that the apples of the province of Quebec were very much superior to those of any other part of the Dominion of Canada.
Of any other place in the world.
I consider that that statement is a very narrow statement for a minister of the Crown to make. I certainly feel justified in criticising and condemning it in the strongest kind of language.
Go ahead.

Because while the minister may take the position that the apples of Quebec are superior, and may believe it, yet such a statement from a minister of the Crown sent broadcast throughout our land, and possibly through other lands, is not justified. It would be wise for him to retract that statement and place himself in a correct position before the people.
Why should the minister be asked to retract it? I do not think there is anything narrow in it. If he believes it to be true that is the statement he ought to make.
Does the hon. gentleman believe it to be true?

It does not make any difference whether I do or not. If the minister believes it to be true he had a right to say so. I have no doubt that if the minis-Mr. FISHER.
ter had been speaking in the Northwest Territories, or in Quebec, or in Ontario, of the wheat of the west he would have said there is no wheat grown in Canada equal to the No. 1 hard.
The hon. gentleman forgets that the apples from the county which he represents bring the highest price in the English markets of any Canadian apples.
I am not arguing that because I have not sufficient knowledge. If the Minister of Agriculture thought that the apples grown in Quebec were the best it was not narrow to express that opinion.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Miller) is in a different position from the Minister of Agriculture. It is quite right for the hon. gentleman to make a statement about fruit grown in his riding, but the Minister of Agriculture is a prominent man to whom the apple growers look for reasonable, and fair statements, and for him to make such a statement is narrow. [DOT]

An opinion expressed by the Minister of Agriculture has more weight than a statement by a private member, but I think the Minister of Agriculture has just as good a right to be frank and honest in the statements he makes as any private member, and it seems to me rather a sign of narrowness to criticise the statement than to make it.
The minister has said that the apples from Quebec are the best in Canada, or in the world. That is his individual opinion.
Yes.

He should get the English buyers, and the buyers of the world to agree with him on that point. The apples from the upland in Grey, over to the Georgian bay are known as Georgian bay fruit in the apple markets in England and Scotland, and bring the be3t price, except the handpicked apples from British Columbia. These are facts that cannot be gainsaid, and it ill becomes the hon. member for Grey to speak as he did. I consider that comparisons of this kind are very odious, as we used to write at the head of our copy books, and I am surprised that the Minister of Agriculture would begin making comparisons as between the products of different sections of the country when they are not borne out by the facts. Does the minister not think it w.ould be better, instead of bringing in a Bill providing for an inspection of, at the most, a casual kind, to stop the importation of seedlings or fruit trees, except those of a special kind that should be admitted by special instructions of the Department of Agriculture? We all

know that some years ago the black knot was introduced in that way, and it has destroyed all the plum and cherry trees, and is to-day to be found in the wild trees along the roadside. Moths of various kinds, the San Jose scale, and other pests have been introduced, and the only way to prevent this is to prevent the importation of seedlings. We can produce plenty of them in this country, and if we keep out the foreign seedlings and grafts of trees of this kind we will be doing the farmers a great benefit. The fruit growers can buy Canadian trees as cheaply as American. The only reason they buy in the United States is because they get the trees cheaply, and to prohibit the importation of seedlings would encourage the nursery business, especially in the province of Quebec, where, I believe, they could grow better nursery stock than can be grown in New York state or any state where they produce this stock. Shut them out for a given time, five or ten years.

My hon. friend is perhaps not familiar with the facts of the case. In the first place this stock came from France, not from the United States. Of the nursery trees grown in Canada, I am well within the mark when I say that not one-tenth of one per cent of them are not grafted on imported stock. Now, if my hon. friend's statement were to be carried out, it would absolutely put a stop, for a number of years, to the growing of nursery stock in Canada. My hon. friend is not aware, perhaps, that this stock -is imported by the nurserymen of Canada in the form of little seedlings, and on these are grafted, when they arrive, the scions taken from Canadian trees. They have not got this stock in Canada.
Why?
Because they do not grow it.
That is, they can buy it abroad cheaper than they can grow it.
Yes.
CURRIE But these seedlings can be grown here.

But, if the nurserymen were debarred from bringing them in, it would stop the growth of Canadian nursery stock for several years. They might get back to it, but they could not do it at the present time. That is the first point. The second point is that the suggestion which my hon. friend makes was carried out with the introduction of the San Jose Scale Act. At that time, we absolutely .prohibited the importation of any trees or stock from the countries infested with the San Jose scale. But the very men on whose behalf my
hon. friend is now speaking petitioned this government and parliament to relax the law and make arrangements by which they could import nursery stock.
Who did that?

The nurserymen, the farmers, the fruit growers-everybody concerned. And the result was that during the next year-I feel confident that it was within eighteen months of the passing of the Act-we had to amend the Act so as to provide stations at which this nursery stock could be imported. I sympathize with the view taken by my hon. friend, but if he will go to the people who are engaged in this business and make the proposition he makes here, 1 am sure he will find them unanimously against it.

That may be so. But it is because it happens to enable them to make a few dollars. Many of these institutions are quite willing to sacrifice the fruit industry of the whole country to make a few dollars for themselves. But the minister should look at it from the point of view of the whole country, and not from the point of view of a special interest. Another point I would like to ask about is whether the minister has taken steps to prevent the importation of potatoes from Newfoundland? For I understand that, according to the report of his own department, the potatoes of Newfoundland are infected with a disease which would ruin the crops in Canada in a very few years.

All the steps have been taken that I have power to take, and I am asking for this Bill to be enabled to take further steps. I have notified the customs authorities, and have asked them to inform my department immediately when entry is made of potatoes from Newfoundland. I do not, think that any have been made, but if any should be made I will send my inspector there to destroy them. I have notified the people of the maritime provinces, who sometimes do get potatoes from Newfoundland-they are the only people in Canada who do-and have told them of the danger and warned them against using any such potatoes. So, I have taken every step that it is competent for me to take. I have not been able to forbid the entry of potatoes from Newfoundland, for the very reason that I have not an Act such as is here proposed. It is because I wish authority to go further that I am asking the House to pass this Bill.
So far, so good.

There are conditions when absolute prohibition may be necessary, but there are others when inspection is necessary, and still others when fumigation is sufficient. This proposed measure will en-

able me to take whichever of these steps seems necessary. I must trust to my expert advisers, the entomologist and the botanist of the experimental farm, who are men of eminence in their several domains, first for information as to the existence of a danger, and second, as to the means to be taken to meet it. Among other things, I ask authority to destroy any infected or infested stock or vegetable matter which may come in, and, when necessary, to destroy packages, and also to grant compensation, as is only fair and right, in some cases to the people who lose thereby. I repeat that if absolute prohibition were exercised to-morrow and the bringing in of these seedlings for the purpose of grafting were completely prohibited, it would paralyze the nursery trade of Canada for some years. I am sure my hon. friend would not wish to do that, and I have no doubt he has spoken without full consideration and without the intimate knowledge which, by reason of my connection with this work, I have necessarily acquired.

I would also ask whether the minister intends to cover grain under this Bill. He might as well take power in relation to seed grain as well. Medical men claim that the corn grown in certain of the states, especially in the southern states, is at present giving humanity a terrible disease known as pellagra. Also, I believe, a great many of the noxious weeds brought into Canada are brought in with foreign grain. The minister should be empowered under this Bill to stop this traffic, as a policeman on the corner stops the road traffic in order to prevent danger!

The Bill covers that. It provides in relation to 'any vegetable matter.' As to weeds, the Seed Control Act applies pretty thoroughly to that, as it covers seeds imported as well as seeds grown in Canada.

I hope the minister (Mr. Fisher) will retract the statement made as to the province of Quebec and the apples grown there. It seems to me a narrow, provincial view for a minister of the Crown of this Dominion to take. The hon. minister represents the whole Dominion, and not one province or a part "of a province only. On what authority does the hon. gentleman base his statement? Let the hon. minister come into the western part of Ontario, even into the district of Grey, represented by the hon. member (Mr. Miller) who took exception to the statement I made some time ago, and he will find that the apples grown there are being disposed of in the markets of the world at prices above even those that the apples of the province of Quebec can command. And, if he will look at the returns, Mr. FISHER.
he will see that a very small proportion of our apples are grown in the province of Quebec. I am really surprised that the minister should take the position he does. As an instance, take my own district. The men who are engaged in the fruit industry there have to take into consideration this fact, that the Minister of Agriculture says that the best apples that can be grown are grown in the province of Quebec, and I suppose he means to infer that the best place to engage in that industry - is the province of Quebec. If that is not a narrow, provincial policy for the minister to take I do not know what a narrow, provincial policy is. The hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Miller; would not dare to go up in his riding and confirm the statement made by the minister.

I will dare to make any statement in my riding that I dare to make here, no matter what it is, and I say again that the hon. gentleman is not as wise on this question as he really thinks he is. I wish that the Minister of Agriculture would come into my riding and say anything that would spur up the agriculturists there to pay much more attention to their orchards than they do.
That has nothing to do with this statement.

It has this to do with it, that it shows that the hon. member for East Lambton does not know the condition in my riding as well as I know it myself. I believe that in my riding they can grow apples to very good advantage, and I believe that if the Minister of Agriculture will come up there, as I trust he will, and say something that will spur the farmers there to greater activity and cause them to take a greater interest in their orchards, it would be very much better for them, and when he comes I want him to be as honest m my riding as he is in the province of Quebec, and if he tells them that while they can grow good apples in Ontario, they can perhaps grow apples of a somewhat better flavour in Quebec, I do not believe that any one will object.
Mr^J. A. CURRIE. How many thousand barrels of apples were shipped out of your county?

Not very many from my riding. In the northern part of the county there may have been a larger quantity-shipped. I do not think that the farmers pay anything like the attention to their orchards, as "a general thing-there may be exceptions-that they ought to.

The statement made by the hon. member for South Grey is far from being in line with the statement made

by the Minister of Agriculture. The statement made by the hon. member for South Grey is that he will ask the Minister of Agriculture to come up into his riding and tell them that they ought to get to work and improve their orchards and perhaps improve the quality of fruit. But what would he think if the minister came up into his riding and said: Gentlemen, though you can produce apples in a way, this place cannot compare with the province of Quebec, because we can produce much better fruit in the province of Quebec than you can here? I have asked the minister, and not the member for South Grey, to answer the question or take back the statement.
I really do not know whether it is worth my while. I am amused by the hon. gentleman's reference to this matter. I cannot imagine that the hon. gentleman, although he looks so serious, is serious.
Yes, Sir, I am serious.

Well, all I can say is that I am sorry for his narrow-mindedness and small comprehension. I have no hesitation in repeating what I said. I may be wrong, the hon. gentleman is welcome to think otherwise, and everybody else is welcome to think otherwise, but I still believe, as far as flavour and quality are concerned, some of the apples grown in the province of Quebec, and the apples generally in Quebec, are the best m the world. I am going to repeat it and repeat it to the hon. gentleman, and I do not care what he thinks about it, one way or the other. He and everybody else may think differently, but I repeat it, as I have repeated it everywhere. I have done it a thousand times, and I am going to do it a thousand times again, whether I am Minister of Agriculture or not, and whether the hon. member criticise me for it or not. I do not think it makes the slightest difference. Where-ever I am, and whenever I am dealing with matters of this kind, I will say just what I think, I will give expression to my opinion to the farmers as to everybody else, and I will defend the interests of the people of Canada in regard to agricultural production to the fullest extent possible. I have my own opinions, and I have my own tastes in regard to things, and I am not going to deny them or withhold them.

I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that after listening to the statement of the Minister of Agriculture, I feel that the vigour of my own remarks was justified. A paper has been read here this afternoon condemning the minister in the strongest possible way, and I cannot help but think that not only will that paper condemn him, but that practically every paper interested in agriculture throughout the country will be strong of the condemnation of his action in this House. The hon. gentleman knows that he has adopted a narrow-minded policy. What authority has a minister of the Crown, who is supposed to represent the people of the Dominion and all of the provinces, to say on the floor of this House that as far as his opinion of the apple growing industry is concerned, the province of Quebec is the place to grow apples?
I did not say that,
That is practically what it meant.

Confine yourself to what
I say.

That is all right, but the minister knows that that is practically the idea that the people in general will get out of the remarks he has made here this afternoon, and I myself emphatically wish to say that it ill-becomes a minister, who represents the different provinces 'of the Dominion, to get up and make such a narrow provincial statement as that.

I think the farmers of my own riding, and even the farmers of the riding of my hon. friend from East Lamb-ton, are sufficiently intelligent to want from the Minister of Agriculture, when he addresses them, either by going before them, or through the press, or from the floor of this House, not flattery but truth.

I rather agree with my hon. friend from East Lambton, and I must say that I am very much surprised at the cautious Minister of Agriculture in stating to us that the province of Quebec is the province in Canada that grows apples of the best flavour. I am not quite sure whether my hon. friend is discharging his duties as Minister of Agriculture in the best possible way when he makes a statement of that kind on the floor of this House. I am not going to offer any criticism as to whether he should hold that opinion or not; that is a matter for himself. Before the Agriculture Committee occasionally very pointed questions are put to the officials of the department who are there giviqg their evidence. When a pointed question is put-such as, which province grows the best wheat?-the official hesitates and says: I do not wish to make any comparisons; I am only here to make a statement of facts. Some of the lessons that my hon. friend has been giving to his officials m the department perhaps might be learned with advantage by himself, and while my hon. friend may say that it is his right to express an opinion, and while it may be endorsed by the hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Miller), who comes from a part of the province where, as he states himself, they

do not pay any very special attention to apple growing, my hon. friend must remember that there are parts of Ontario
where they are devoting a great deal of attention to apple raising, and where there are very large exporters, such as there are in one part of my own county, where men have a thousand trees, some a great many more, and where they sell the output of their orchards for $2,500 and $3,000. These men are very much interested in the apple export trade. I am not quite sure that my hon. friend is giving fair play to other parts of Canada when he allows it to go abroad from his high position in the government of this country that he has no hesitation to state on the floor of this House from which province the best apples come, which are being sent to the old country. I think my hon. friend has rather forgotten his usual caution. For myself, I agree with my hon. friend from East Lamb-ton, and I do not agree with the hon. member for South Grey m this matter. It may be that my hon. friend's constituents require a little prodding up. I think they do in many ways. If the agricultural interests of his constituency are not taken care of, he must blame either himself or the Minister of Agriculture, and not the member for East Lambton, who is advocating the principle that the Minister of Agriculture, having a better opportunity than any other single man in Canada to protect agricultural interests, should not single out any one province and say that it produced the best apples for export trade and home consumption, thus instituting an invidious and injurious comparison. That is going a little beyond his duties, and I do not think it will be endorsed by the people. The hon. gentleman is used to having the commendation of the people of Canada.
Hear hear.
But there were other days-
Before they had the experience.
But there were other days coming, and perhaps the Minister of Agriculture will learn bv experience later on.

I certainly would not have spoken on this question were it not for the statement which the Minister of Agriculture has made on the floor of the House. I can quite understand that as a minister for the province of Quebec, and speaking to a Quebec audience, he might assume an optimistic tone as regards the conditions in that province, and I would not take exception to what he said then. But, when he speaks from his place in parliament as a minister (of the Crown and when, in cold blood he reiterates the (statement that the province of Quebec does grow the best apples, thus making invidious comparisons between the provinces of Mr. BLAIN.
the Dominion, I do think it is at least an error of judgment on the part of the minister. Naturally my people will see these reports in the press, and coming as I do from what I think to be the best fruit growing district in the best fruit country in the Dominion of Canada.
Oh, you ought not to say that.

Coming as I do from what I believe to be the best fruit growing district in Canada, my people would very properly want to know why I allowed an expression of that kind to pass without protest. I do not pretend to be an expert as is my friend from Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Burrell) but I would direct the attention of the Minister of Agriculture to the fact that within the last two years they have established in the city of Spokane what is claimed to be the largest exclusively apple show on the continent of America and perhaps in the world, and at that show at which apples from all parts of the continent competed, my particular district received a large number of the first prizes in many lines. The district of Kootenay, my own particular district, received the first award for apples at the Spokane apple exhibition. Again, the minister well knows, (for if I am not mistaken I have seen it in one of the government reports) that the province of British Columbia took the gold medal at the British show, and only last year that province was awarded a special medal for the best 50 boxes of the best fruit and the best packed fruit. I do not know if the province of Quebec was represented there, but if so I would be only too delighted to hear that it also received an award, because, I do not think that in a great country such as ours there is room for these small jealousies and invidious comparisons. I feel that the remarks made by the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) were only faiT and I was rather surprised at the attitude assumed bv the Minister of Agriculture in replying to him. I like to hear a minister representing a province in this great Dominion giving words of encouragement to his own people, and I would not take very great exception to what was said by the hon. gentleman in his own province of Quebec, but when the minister reads in Hansard, the statement he has made on the floor of the House and which he does not withdraw, that there is no other province in which they grow apples on the whole equal in quality and flavour to the apples grown in the province of Quebec, I think the hon. gentleman will, on reflection, admit that from his own standpoint and the standpoint of the country, he has made a mistake.

I would remind my hon. friend that although I am Minister of Agri-

culture I am still the representative of a county in Quebec; and if the hon. gentleman is permitted to say that his part of British Columbia grows the best fruit and is the best fruit growing district in Canada, I do not see why I should not be permitted to make the same claim for my own province.

There is a great difference and the minister knows it. It is one thing for a private member to say that in his opinion his district grows the best apples in Canada, but while the Minister of Agriculture represents a county in Quebec he has a wider field and is a minister of the Crown for the whole Dominion He can very well see that when the English importers of apples, having British Columbia fruit on hand, advertise the statement made by the Minister of Agriculture in parliament, it might be a serious detriment to the fruit coming from other provinces. Then, the minister has not attempted. to support his statement by any documentary evidence.
I simply gave my own opinion, my own taste.
Your taste may be vitiated.

If the minister could show that in competition with the fruit of other parts of Canada the apples of the province of Quebec had carried off all the awards, then he might have some foundation for the statement.
I told the hon. gentleman over and over again that I gave my own opinion and my own taste and nothing more.

I have nothing to do with the hon. gentleman's taste, but I have something to do with his opinion as Minister of Agriculture. When my hon. friend repeats and re-repeats in this House that in his opinion the best apples produced in Canada are from the province of Quebec, he makes that statement as Minister of Agriculture, and in so doing I have no hesitation in saying that he is not giving fair play to every other province in Canada. I would have no hesitation myself in expressing my opinion that the best apples to be found in the world are to be found in the province of Ontario.
Just the same as I have.

No, I occupy an entirely different position. I am merely a humble representative of a constituency in the province of Ontario, while my hon. friend is Minister of Agriculture. When the people of the world are looking for a statement in regard to the agricultural capabilities of this country, they are not looking for it from an ordinary member of this House;
they look for it from a man in authority like the Minister of Agriculture. Time and again, in the Committee on Agriculture, when questions- have been put to officers of his own department, as to which province produced the best of this or the best of that, my hon. friend has always said, you must not make comparisons, and the committee endorsed him; because it would not do for any official, who is an official of all Canada, to make a statement, even in the Committee on Agriculture, that one province produced better crops of fruit or potatoes or anything -else than 'another province. My hon. friend recognized the propriety of that, and he would not go through the country and make statements of that kind. He is too good a politician for that. And if my hon. friend will not allow the ordinary officials of hia department to single out one province aa being superior to another in this respect, my hon. friend as Minister of Agriculture should not on the floor of this House single out one province, and say that it produces better apples than any other province in Canada.

In the absence of Sir Frederick Borden, representing Kings county, and in the absence of Dr. Black, representing the county of Hants, and in the absence of Mr. Pickup, representing the county of Annapolis, I am bound to stand up for the province of Nova Scotia; and the first thing I want to say is that the hon. Minister of Agriculture has- no right to assume that he occupies the same position as the hon. member for Peel or any other member who represents a county in this House. The Minister of Agriculture represents the whole Dominion. I am sorry for him, but nevertheless he does.
We cannot help it.

I cannot help it now, but I hope some day to help it. My hon. friend, however, need not feel so safe that he can come here and make any statement he likes. My hon. friend said a moment ago that he had as much right to say that the best apples were grown in Quebec as the hon. member from British Columbia had to say that the best apples were grown in that province. I say that neither has the right to say anything of the kind unless he has the facts to back up the statement.
How about Nova Scotia?

My hon. friend knows enough about Nova Scotia to know that it is a straight statement that the best ap- . pies in the world come from Nova Scotia. Any man who knows anything about fruit knows that Nova Scotia apples do not take second place to any apples in the world.



If the hon. minister had said that the apples grown, in Quebec, were as good as any grown anywhere else in the Dominion of Canada, no one would find fault with him; but to say that the best apples are grown in Quebec is I think, quite unfair and unreasonable, in view of the fact, which he knows himself, that apples from Nova Scotia are at least not second to any grown in Quebec or in the world. I am not an apple grower, but I am an apple eater, and I think I have a better taste than the Minister of Agriculture. I think his taste must have been interfered with when he was eating those apples.
What time of the evening was it?

I do not know what time of the evening it was, but I always eat apples in a reasonable hour. I have not had the pleasure of eating any apples grown in Quebec, but I have eaten apples grown in Nova Scotia, and I am quite sure that the province of Quebec cannot beat the province of Nova Scotia in the production of apples or in their quality.
Mr. FISHER Hear, hear.

And the Minister of Agriculture agrees with me; so he has taken back what he said. I have no desire that Nova Scotia apples should be stated by the Minister of Agriculture or anybody else to be the best that are grown, but I say that thev are equal to any that are grown, and anybody who watches the market knows that there are none that bring a higher price; and that is not a question of taste, but a question of ' money talks.'

I am very sorry that I have to differ with members on this side of the House who have spoken. I quite agree with the Minister of Agriculture that the best apples are grown in the province of Quebec. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Crosby) talks about taste. I really thought he had better taste. But I must say that I think the Minister of Agriculture has better taste as regards apples than the hon. member for Halifax.

This discussion has been a revelation to me because I thought it was thoroughly and generally understood that the best apples in the country were produced in the county of North Grey and that it was one of these which caused the mischief between Adam and Eve, but I must admit that the British Columbia members have the best of us because I understand that the apple which Eve ate was B. C.

I have here a photograph which I want to show the Minister of Agriculture of apples shipped to my constituency this year. I think this photograph is really worth being, presented to this House. This photograph was taken not by myself, but under my direction, of apples packed in Ontario and sent out to the northwest.

I really think the hon. minister should withdraw the statement he has just made. There is no reason in the world why a minister of the Crown, representing the whole Dominion, should make a statement of that kind. Such a statement will be used in the markets of the world as an advertisement. Is it statesmanlike on the part of the hon. gentleman to advertise certain districts where apples are grown in this country, and have it go out to the world on his authoritv that Quebec is the place where the best apples are grown in the Dominion?
That was the apple of discord, apparently.

Apple sauce as far as the Minister of Agriculture is concerned. I hope that he will have the decency to withdraw that statement. He is well aware that in Ontario we raised some 15,000,000 barrels last year, which is the largest amount of apples grown by any province; but if the Quebec shippers can put a stamp on the apples they send to Great Britain to the effect that the Minister of Agriculture of this country stated emphatically on the floor of parliament that the apples grown in that province are the best in the Dominion, you may depend upon it the Quebec apples will thereby gain an advantage over those of the other provinces. I would like the hon. minister to at least state whether he is going to withdraw that statement.
Carried.
I would ask him what authority he has for making it?
Carried.
I have asked a reasonable and fair question, and I think the minister ought at least to give an answer.
I have answered the hon. gentleman and am not going to answer him any more on that subject.

That is certainlv a verv strange position to take. We are well aware that the hon. gentleman has made some statements ill becoming a minister of the Crown. I am sure that when he sees those statements in print to-morrow, he will regret having made them. I represent a large agricultural district where quantities of the verv best apples in the Dominion are grown, and I feel it my duty to point out to the minister that he has been making statements contrary to the best interests of the apple growing industry. I sincerely hope that during recess he will take the opportunity to reflect and that when we resume at 8 o'clock he will have come to the conclusion that he had better admit he has made a mistake and is willing to show fair play to the whole of the Dominion.
At six o'clock, committee took recess.
After Recess. [DOT]
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.

I hope since the minister has had his dinner he will be in a little better humour, and will withdraw the remark he made in reference to the apple industry, and also the insulting remarks he made about myself. I did not know until after the House had risen that he had made use of the words that I was narrow-mind-1794
ed, and of small comprehension. If he thinks that is becoming to a minister of the Crown, it is high time we placed him where he belongs. He considers that he is at liberty to come into this House and bulldoze, and browbeat members as he would perhaps some of his own constituents in the province of Quebec. It is high time he realized the position he holds in the House. I will ask the minister if he will be good enough to withdraw that statement.
No.

Then I say his words ill become a minister of the Crown in the House of Commons. In referring to the hon. gentleman I took care not to make a personal reference, I said that his policy on this question was a narrow and provincial policy. In the face of that the hon. gentleman says: Your remarks are narrow-minded, and of small comprehension. Will he say the same about the Montreal ' Star ' or this ' Fruit Journal ', or the dozens of fruit journals or agricultural papers that will attack the statement of the minister, and criticise it in its proper light. Are they narrow-minded and small of comprehension? If the hon. gentleman will look over his record he will see what a narrow-minded policy he has been carrying on ever since he took office. Let him go back to his position as manufacturing squirt guns to feed chickens and scissors to cut peaches off the trees, and his primitive cold storage apparatus. Follow him all down through his career, and you cannot come to any other conclusion than that it ill becomes him to make such statements of an hon. member. Has the hon. gentleman seen this statement in this paper referring to his statement in Quebec, and in British Columbia?
That certain varieties of the apple are more successful in certain parts of the fruit-growing area of the Dominion than in others is true, but to make the broad statement that ' the flavour of the British Columbia apple was not to be compared with that of the province of Quebec,' or vice versa, is certainly taking a rash plunge into the deep and chilly waters of odious comparisons.
The hon. gentleman made use of these words this afternoon:
I consider the apples of Quebec, as far as flavour and quality are concerned, to be better than anything produced not only in British Columbia but in the whole world.
If the hon. gentleman was a private member of the House it would be a very different question, but he is a minister of the Crown, and ha3 to deal with the different districts throughout the Dominion. Let us carry that to its legitimate conclusion, let him, if he dares, pick out certain qualities of agricultural products produced on the farms of Canada, and say that they are

adapted altogether to one certain province. He knows he would not dare to take any such position as that, but he thinks it proper to take that position in reference to the great apple industry. Only a few years ago we produced 20,000,000 barrels of apples and 15,000,000 of these were produced in Ontario, and the minister would place a stigma on the apples of that province by stating that those of Quebec are superior; he is simply as it were, advertising, or booming the products of one province in direct opposition to the products of another province. If the minister has not the manliness or backbone, or good judgment to withdraw the words he used, I leave it to the judgment of the House as to who is the man of narrow mind and little comprehension. I am satisfied they will leave it not very far from the Minister of Agriculture.

I was, I must confess, a little surprised this afternoon to near the statement of the Minister of Agriculture in resDect to the apples of Quebec. While I have a verv high admiration for the various farming communities and horticultural communities of this Dominion, at the same time I do not think it is wise or seemly, or fair, that a gentleman occupying the position of Minister of Agriculture of Canada should single out any particular province for his commendation. His statement was: ' I consider the apples of Quebec, as far as flavour and quality are concerned, to be infinitely superior to anything produced, not only in British Columbia, but in the whole world.' So long as [DOT] this difference was only between the hon. member for Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Burrell) and the hon. minister, and affected only the provinces of British Columbia and Quebec, I felt it no duty of mine to make any comment with respect to it; but when the minister made so broad and sweeping a statement as he finally did, it seemed that in justice to the province of Nova Scotia, which has an enviable record with respect to the fruits produced there, I should enter a protest. I do not know whether the minister has visited that province of recent years, and ha3 seen the fruit which is grown there?
Yes.

If the minister has, I fear that his observations of the Annapolis valley, and other sections, must have been of 'a' very cursory nature, or else he has done an injustice to that province with his eyes open, because the Annapolis valley, as a fruit growing district, is not excelled by any part of Canada. I feel it is only right, on behalf of the fruit growers of the Annapolis valley, and other sections, that I should enter a protest against the statement of the minister, and say that I Mr. ARMSTRONG.
do not think that their fruit is excelled in any part of the Dominion.	,
I make that statement, of course, as a private member. I have not had the same opportunity as the minister to visit all parts of the Dominion where fruit is grown, but I make the statement as the result of reading such reports as have been available, and after such investigation as it has been within my power to make. I think it would be well if the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), who representes that province, the hon. member for Hants, (Mr. Black), the Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Borden), representing, as he does, the county of Kings, and the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Pickup), were to rise and endorse the statement I make that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) has, possibly all unwittingly, done the province of Nova Scotia, and particularly the Annapolis valley, and other fruit growing sections a grave and serious injustice in the sweeping statement which I have just recited. Such a statement, coming from the Minister of Agriculture, comes as an authoritative statement; and it goes out not only to the people of Canada, but to the people of the whole world as the statement of one who might well be said to be in the position of an expert, and to make the statement as a result of investigation, and inquiry, and with the very fullest knowledge that it is possible for any man in Canada to possess. And because of that, it becomes my duty to challenge, and I do challenge the statement which the Minister of Agriculture has made, so far at least as the province of Nova Scotia is concerned. The fruitgrowers of the Annapolis valley and adjoining sections about which I am specially concerned, and about which I know most, have been doing a splendid work during the past few years. They have been raising an excellent variety of fruit, and placing that fruit on the market in the best of condition, gaining thereby a most enviable reputation. I do not think it fair or just-yes, I agree with the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) in saying that I think it is not seemly- for the Minister of Agriculture to discriminate in his remarks against the fruitgrowers of Nova Scotia, as he did. I am sure the Minister of Agriculture will not misunderstand me in making that statement. He will understand that I am merely doing what I believe to be my duty to the people of Nova Scotia, and the fruit growers of the districts I have mentioned. It may not be a very agreeable task for one to gainsay a statement of an hon. minister who should have full knowledge of the subject on which he speaks, but I only regard it as a duty, and I trust that other hon. members from the apple-growing districts of Nova Scotia will endorse my statement

and will join with me in asking the Minister of Agriculture to modify at least, if he will not withdraw, the statement he has made in view of the fact that it is undoubtedly a discrimination against the province of Nova Scotia, and an unfair discrimination, and that it will prove a detriment to these apple-growers when they seek to place their fruit on the market.

This appears to be a little worse than a temnest in a tea-pot. When I came in, and heard the excited and exciting declamation of the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong), I thought that surely the Minister of Agriculture had been guilty at least of high treason. Surely, for a man to praise the fruit of his own county is no crime. I myself represent the county that grows the best fruit in the world, yet I do not imagine for a moment that the Minister of Agriculture or the member for East Lambton is going to take offence at my saying so. I think it is a very loyal thing for a man to believe that his own country is the best, and that the apples grown near his own door are better than any others.
Does the hon. member (Mr. Black) think that the influence his statement will exert will be as widespread as that exerted by the statement of the Minister of Agriculture?

Some of the members on the other side are cultivating a very bad habit. The moment a man gets up on this side to speak, they immediately ask questions. Now I like to make my speech in my own way. I do not speak very often, and I think I set a very good example to some of the newer and younger members on the other side who rise on every question. I would not take part in this discussion were it not that-I say it truthfully and without boasting-I represent one of the best fruit counties in Canada. Indeed, 'as a pastime, I have been a fruit grower myself. It is a very profitable business in my county. I would as soon own a good fruit orchard in the county of Hants as own stock in the Bank of Nova Scotia. I am sorry I was out for a few minutes this afternoon, so that the apple industrv had to be defended by that eminent fruit grower the hon. member for the city of Halifax (Mr. Crosby). I am sorry also that this duty of defence had to be assumed by the hon. member for Digby (Mr. Jameson). If it had been a question of Digby chickens, or smoked herring, or dried fish, the hon. member for Digby would certainly be in a good position to speak. But I have always noticed, as soon as I crossed the line of Annapolis county going west, that the apple blossoms cease and the apple'trees were nowhere to be found in the county of Digby.
The hon. gentleman must have had his eyes closed.

No, I have gone there many times, and I have not seen much farming land there. They have a splendid summer resort, they have the magnificent Annapolis basin to look at, and many other fine things, but they do not grow fruit, and it is not a farming county. The Annapolis valley would seem to be the fruit growing district of Nova Scotia according to the hon. member for Digby. But the Annapolis valley is a little strip of Nova Scotia about twenty-five or thirty miles long; the great fruit-growing belt takes in the county of Hants and the county of Kings, neither of which have anything to do with the Annapolis valley. Indeed, there are four or five great apple growing valleys in Nova Scotia. There are the Annapolis valley, the Cornwallis valley, which, perhaps, produces the greatest quantity of any part of Nova Scotia, and which is in the county of Kings, the Gaspereau valley, which is noted for its beauty and its apple growing all over eastern Canada; the Avon valley in my own county, and many others where fruit is grown. I will not take up time now; this is a trifling discussion, and almost unworthy the members taking part in it. I take no offence at what the Minister of Agriculture has said concerning the apples of his province. He deserves credit for standing by his own. I say as much for the apples oi my own province, and I do not think that anybody would take offence at that. I am glad that so many parts of Canada can show to the world such splendid results in apple-growing. We export from Nova Scotia 750,000 barrels to London alone, and we are increasing that year by year, and are capable of growing at least twenty times the quantity we now grow. Orchards are increasing and new orchards are being set out. Men come in to buy the apples, m fact, they will advance you money on your fruit. They tumble over one another in trying to get your apples.

I do not propose to discuss this question at any great length. Of course, in Ontario, we think we grow the best apples that are grown in the Dominion. especially in the county of Oxford. I know that in Nova Scotia they grow very fine apples. I think their Gravensteins will compare favourably with some of our best apples. They have very beautiful looking apples in British Columbia. I think they beat us as far as appearance goes; I will not say as far as flavour goes, because I never tasted many of their apples, but certainly they grow nice looking apples. I know that they grow exceptionally fine apples on the island of Montreal, and especially the Fameuse, which is perhaps equal to anything grown in Canada in more

ways than one. I was not here this afternoon, and I am not very well posted on what has been said, but evidently there is some feeling regarding a statement that the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) has made with respect to the quality of apples grown in the province of Quebec. I think the question is viewed entirely from the wrong standpoint, ana that is the point I wish to make. If the province of Quebec is growing the very best apples in the Dominion of Canada so much the better for the rest of the Dominion. If the province of British Columbia has better apples than any other part of the Dominion so much the better for Ontario, Nova Scotia and Quebec. If we have the best apples in Ontario it is better for every other province that we have the best or at least good apples. The better the apples we produce the better it will be for every province in the Dominion. If the minister says that the apples grown in the province of Quebec are the best, he has not done us any injury in Ontario, but he has done us good. Place 100,000 barrels of apples on the market in Liverpool and if they are all good you can get rid of them at a good, big price, and follow them with another 100,000 barrels and get another big price for those. But if half of them are poor all the good apples the following week will bring less money, because there were poor apples placed on the market the previous week. If we can give the impression abroad that any other province is producing better apples than we are it will only be an incentive for us to do better and to try and produce good apples in every province of the Dominion. Instead of the minister being open to criticism he has a perfect right to say that apples in one province, for some reasons, suit his taste or idea better than the apples of another province. I would not hesitate to express an opinion myself regarding the apples of any province if I thought they were the best, whether it was in Nova Scotia, British Columbia, Ontario, or Quebec.

It is not the question of which province grows the best apples that we are here to discuss. The Minister of Agriculture is not the Minister of Agriculture of Nova Scotia, Quebec, or Ontario or any other province, but of this Dominion, has made a statement without producing anything to back it up or to show that it is a statement of fact, and that is the question that we are discussing at the present moment. The hon. member for Hants (Mr. Black) has said that he was sorry that the defence of the fruitgrowing industry of Nova Scotia had been left in the hands of the hon. member for Halifax. I can only tell him that there was no member from that part of the province on that side of the House to look Mr. SCHELL.
after the matter when it came up. I confess that I am not an apple grower, but I am an apple eater. If the hon. member for Hants had the facts before him as had the hon. member for Digby (Mr. Jameson) he would have understood distinctly what the hon. gentleman had said.
I heard the Minister of Agriculture, because I was here when he made the statement.
Then you should have been here to defend your province.
I was glad I was out when some of the speeches were made.

The hon. member for Hants was born and brought up in a county that is noted for raising peaches. The Minister of Agriculture makes himself a judge for this whole Dominion and undertakes to declare that the best apples are raised in Quebec. 1 am not here to say a word against the apples in Quebec. I have no doubt they raise as good apples in Quebec as they raise any place else, but the minister has no right to make that statement in this House. If he were to make that statement in the province of Quebec we might forgive him, because he is given to saying one thing in one province and another in another. But we cannot forgive him when he comes into this House, and, in cold blood, makes a statement such as he did make and which is without foundation. I believe that if the Minister of Agriculture made a slip he should not be so stubborn as not to stand up and say: Well, boys, from all the other provinces, forgive me; I did not Know what I was saying and X_ will take it all back. One of two things he must do; he must take that statement back or prove it by some facts, because he is not supposed to be a judge of apples. He may be constituted as Minister of Agriculture, through no fault of mine, but he has never been appointed by anybody as a judge of apples, and he must either take the statement back or produce evidence to show that it is a statement of fact. They ao have fish in the county I come from, and I would advise some hon. members on the other side of the House to eat a little fish. If what they say about fish is true, they need a little. We raise apples m Halifax county, but we have so many other things that we pride ourselves on that we do not particularly worry about our apples. It is unfair that the statement which the minister has made should go abroad. We forgive the minister when he goes to Quebec and makes a statement of that kind, and I believe that they will forgive him there for it, he might make it when he goes to Ontario, but I do not think he has any right to make it in this House.

(Translation.) Mr. Chairman, I am surprised that many members of the opposition who have discussed this matter should ask the hon. Minister of Agriculture to withdraw the statement he made last fall at the pomologicial convention, that the best apples in Canada and even in the whole world, are raised in the province of Quebec.
