The minister, in introducing this Bill to-day, referred to an insect known as the brown-tail moth. This insect has been in some way introduced into the western part of the province of Nova Scotia within the last three or four years, and has been giving a good deal of trouble there. I do not know just how it was introduced. I do not think that it was traced to any fruit trees that were brought in. The statement was made to me by some people who had made very careful investigation of the matter that so far as they could learn it was brought in by some steamer trading between some United States_port, I think Boston, and one of the ports in western Nova Scotia. It secured quite a foothold there before it was recognized, and thereafter some efforts were put forward by the provincial authorities, which although they were fairly vigorous, do not seem to have altogether checked1 its spread and development. The question suggests itself to my mind that as there is a danger of the introduction of this pest in some other way than by bringing in of fruit trees, possibly the minister may have some information in regard to the matter generally which would be useful if it were placed oil ' Hansard ' at this point.

Mv hon. friend is quite correct. I am not able to say offhand just when the pest was introduced into Nova Scotia, and I do not think I have had any knowledge of how it was introduced. But I think the cause suggested by my hon. friend is quite probable, because this moth has been known to obtain a foothold in the New England states some years before it was known in Nova Scotia. The Nova Scotia government has, I think, now three men employed in trying to stamp out the pest. The entomologist of the department

here is in constant touch with them, and is giving them advice, and the late Dr. Fletcher, the late ent-omoffigist of the department, visited Nova Scotia, and described the moth and its habits and helped the paonle there by# advice, information and instruction to combat it; but up to the present time there lias been no law under which we could take any steps to stamp it out. This law will provide the necessary machinery for that work. I wish, without in any way interfering with or depreciating the effort of the provincial government, to help them in every possible way, and as soon as this Bill passes into law, I think we shall be able to work very effectively. Such a case as that mentioned might be one in which I might have to appoint an officer to aid the local authorities, or to carry out the provisions of this law, which might be more effective, especially in a case of the introduction from abroad of an insect pest, than a provincial or local law would be.

I am pleased to hear that statement of the minister. I think it will be of very great assistance if he does make a move along that line. The pest was not very much known in this country until it was introduced into Nova Scotia three or four years ago, and the seriousness of it was not realized until a year or two had elapsed. It is a very serious pest, and any measures that would tend to stamp it out should be taken. In the county of Digby, although my hon. friend from Hants does not seem t-o have remembered it, we raise a good many apples, and I may say that the fruit is of a very excellent quality, particularly in the districts of Bear river, Hill Grove, Acaciaville, and other places. In these districts specimens of this moth have been found; and so far as I have been able to learn it has not only been spreading amongst the fruit trees, but is believed to have taken hold of the general forest growth. I do not know whether that is really the case or not, as I am not sufficiently well informed respecting the habits of this moth; but at all events there is a very suspicious looking insect, which bears a close resemblance in many particulars to the brown-tail moth. I would like to ask the minister whether this moth has beqn discovered in any of the other provinces of Canada, and if so, what measure of success has been met with in the endeavour to stamp it out?

I would say to my hon. friend, in the first place, that this moth does not attack only fruit trees. It attacks all forest trees and shade trees just as much as it attacks fruit trees, except that it does not attack conifers; but deciduous trees it does attack. The moth is not known to exist anywhere except in that Mr. FISHER.
region. Nests have been discovered in some nursery stock, and this has been destroyed. I think my hon. friend was not here this afternoon when I explained that this year and last year we have been fighting this pest without any law. We have been aided, and very handsomely aided, by the importers of nursery stock, who have been willing to have our inspectors inspect their importations, although we had no authority to do so, and they consented to the destruction of such stock as- was affected. It was stated that this winter, during the importing season of nursery stock, we have inspected 1,700,000 seedling trees, and that 293 nests were found, in each of which there might have been from 200 to 300 caterpillars. These were all destroyed. Similar work was done last year. If they had been allowed to come in, there is no dcrubt that by this time the moth would have been thoroughly established in different parts of Canada. The permission of the people to allow us to do that work was purely voluntary. It is in consequence of that experience that I am introducing this Bill. I have here the last farm report for 1909, and it says:
In 1902, Mr. William McIntosh, of St. John, New Brunswick, took a single male specimen of the brown-tail moth (euproctis chry-sor'rhoEia, L.) about 20 miles from St. John, New Brunswick. About the same time another specimen was taken by Mr. Gordon Leavitt, at St. John; and in July of 1905, Mr. John Russell took a third specimen at Digby, Nova Scotia. Up to the present time these have been the only authentic records of this much-to-be-dreaded insect having been taken in Canada. Recently, however, I have received from Mr. C. Perry Foote, of Lakeville, Nova Scotia, one of the winter nests of the brown-tail moth, filled with the living caterpillars, thus proving that this insect has established itself at one place at least in Canada.
Dr. Saunders, in his report, says:
With the exception of the San Jose scale, there are no two insects which have attracted so much public attention, nor with regard to which so much money has been spent in America by the state and federal governments of the United States, as the Gypsy moth and the brown-tail moth. Both of these are pests introduced into America from Europe-the Gypsy moth about 1869, and the brown-tail moth somewhere about 1890. Millions of dollars have now been spent on fighting the Gypsy moth and the brown-tail moth in Massachusetts and the adjoining states. Dr. Howard, when treating of this insect and of an effort which is being made to introduce European parasites says, in the Year-book of the Department of Agriculture for 1905; ' The brown-tail moth has become even more abundant and injurious than the Gypsy moth, and, owing to the fact that the female flies readily, whereas the female of the Gypsy moth does not fly at all, the brown-tail moth has far exceeded the Gypsy moth in its spread/

It is this we are trying to fight against, and it is necessary to give us the *power to do this effectively. I again give credit to the importers of nursery stock for the manner in which they have co-operated with us in keeping the moth out, but at the same time in case of objection, we must take power to do this authoritatively.

I am glad the Minister of Agriculture has read that statement from the report. If the seriousness of this pest were fully understood by the nurserymen and orchardists of this country generally, as we are beginning to understand it in Nova Scotia, I feel sure -that their assistance would be given to the department and to the minister in every effort he makes to stamp it out. If it got a foothold in this country, it would mean that the work of years, I might say the work of generations, would in a measure go for naught, so far as fruit raising is concerned.
I am glad to know that an energetic effort will now be made to destroy this pest in the country. I understood the minister to say that when he gets the legislative authority he thought it likely he would appoint an officer who would act in Nova Scotia, either in conjunction with or independently of the provincial authorities. I trust the minister will appoint that officer, and appoint him as soon as possible, so .that the most vigorous measures will be taken to aid the provincial authorities in reducing, in numbers, if not altogether exterminating this pest.

I may be able to do the work with my present staff, but if the present staff is not sufficient, I will consider it to be my duty to appoint an officer. Last year, and again this year, circulars were sent to a list of about 25,000 orchardists, which we keep in the department, drawing attention to the dangers of this moth and how to detect it. In the agricultural press, and in the press generally throughout the country, information of a similar kind was published, and I believe it is largely due to our efforts that during the last few years, so far as we know, the moth has- not become established in Canada.
On subsection (d),
Why does the minister propose to give compensation to those who are sending in nursery stock from the other side, which is not fit to come into the country?

The loss would generally fall upon our own people. We believe that the cases and the packing in which the nursery stock comes will be pretty sure to contain moths, and consequently we think it necessary to destroy them. The owners complain that they would have been able to use this packing again and that its destruction was a serious loss to them. If these
things are destroyed in the interests of the public at large the owners ought to be compensated in the same way as we compensate owners of animals when we order their destruction. If we did not give compensation, it is not likely that our efforts would be very enthusiastically seconded.

Would not the granting of this compensation be just as likely to make them careless about the goods they pack? If it is only the boxes and casings that are involved, they would only amount to about $2.
It would include compensation for the stock also if that were destroyed.

In our province we have never given any compensation ^ but of course I am not referring to exceptional cases such as the brown-tail moth. Where we destroy, as we do sometimes, quite a heavy percentage of nursery stock importation, we give no compensation, and the importers usually insist on the goods being, sold under a guarantee to pass inspection.

The brown-tail moth has been discovered in shipments which come almost altogether from France, and the practice in the French trade is that the goods must be paid for before shipment. The importers have these two seasons suffered very considerable loss, which they have voluntarily undergone, although they protested very strongly that it was veTy unfair that they should not only lose the stock itself but the packages as well. But we found it absolutely necessary to destroy the packages as well as the stock because the eggs might just as well come in the packages. If no compensation be given, the temptation would be great to avoid the law, and it would be impossible to indentify these packages when used in enveloping other goods.
Is the minister applying compensation only to this particular case of the brown tail moth?
I would not like to say that. That would depend on the conditions and circumstances. I might find similar reasons for compensation in other cases.

The hon. gentleman will see that if the Dominion is going to compensate for all the nursery stock . destroyed, that would make it rather em-barassing for our province which gives no compensation, but of course, I admit that in certain circumstances it would be only fair to compensate.

Suppose, for instance, a certain potato disease, which has been discovered in Newfoundland, should find its

way to Canada, it would be my duty to destroy any crop of potatoes infected in order to prevent that disease from spreading; and it would be rather hard to enter on a man's farm and destroy his crop without giving him some compensation.

I am not opposing the principle because I admit that in certain special cases, it would be only just to compensate, but I would like to know whether that compensation is to be general. In the case of the San Jose scale, for example, the hon. gentleman would not compensate. What other particular cases are there in which he would?
I would not undertake t< say what cases absolutely should be compensated _ and what not. That will have to be decided by order in council.

Why should not the inspection take place in the country from
which the importation comes? How would it do to have a regulation requiring a certificate from a qualified inspector in the country where the goods were bought9 That certificate could be forwarded with the goods.
stroyed and no compensation paid. Then the exporters of these fruit trees would be more particular. If we are going to compensate to the extent of two-thirds of the value, these people would send over any amount of diseased stuff which they could not sell in their own country and get two-thirds of its value; I think the importer should be held responsible and should look to the man from whom he is buying to sell to him an article that would pass government inspection here, making that a condition of payment. Then, if no compensation for stock destroyed was granted, a better quality would be sent to Canada.
We do not destroy the stock but only the packages and packing.
Is there no danger of this brown-tail moth escaping from the packages before the shruibs are inspected?
They could not get out of the packages.
Thev should be inspected immediately on arrival here to avoid that.

We would then be at the mercy of inspectors over whom we have no control. When the San Jose Scale Act was introduced, it was suggested that we might accept the certificate of, United States inspectors, but I was not quite prepared to do that. I prefer to have our own inspection than accept certificates from a class of men of whose appointments and qualifications we knew nothing.
Suppose vou had your own inspection in addition when the goods arrive?

I have just been informed that in seeding stock imported from France, in which were found a large number of nests of the brown-tail moth, every case was stamped with the official statement that the brown-tail moth had no existence in the region from which that nursery stock was shipped.

Was the certificate by some qualified appointee of the Franco government?
Mr.	^es>
it is the certificate
of the Minister of Agriculture for the arrondisement from which the shipment came.

Is it not a little out of the usual to compensate importers who bring in diseased stock? I would suggest that the importer should be responsible and that any fruit trees imported from France or the United States, which did not pass government inspection, should be de-1 Mr. FISHER.
They are inspected as soon as possible.
I move that no compensation be received for the boxes in which they are packed or the packings. It seems folly to attempt to pay foreigners for boxes and packing which amount to only $2 or $3.

If this moth is as dangerous as the minister has represented, would it not be better to entirely prohibit the importation of trees or shrubbery from infected countries altogether? That would not only keep out the moth but would give employment to a large number of people and encourage a new branch of industry.

This Bill gives me that power which I have not at present. That stock is- raised iby the million in France and exported to the United States and Canada, and as I have said the prohibition of its importation would put a stop to the nursery business for some years. We tried the prohibition of importation when first combatting the San Jose scale, but as I have explained the fruit interests made such strong representations that we were obliged to establish stations where stock could be imported and fumigated.

If the exporter were required to make good to the customer in Canada stock destroyed on account of this moth, the exporter would be very careful in the stock he sent to Canada. But, if the importer were allowed compensation

and the exporter -were thus freed from the loss, he would not take the same care. I think it would be worth the minister's while to consider whether it would not give better results if no compensation were allowed. I think this was a little different from the Diseases of Animals Act cited by the Minister of Agriculture, for in such cases the disease develops through no fault of the exporter, and yet may affect the whole country. But, in the case of this stock, the exporter is directly responsible. There is competition among the exporters whether in France or in any other country, and, if a man sends out stock that has to 'be destroyed on reaching Canada, knowing that the importer will probably, try to find some other sources of supply, he will be more likely to grant compensation to the importer. Looking at it purely as a commercial transaction, I think it would be a mistake for the country to decide to give compensation as a general thing. It would probably encourage rather than discourage carelessness in the shipping of stock into the country. I may be wrong, but that is the way it appeals to me.

Some ol the older members of this House will remember Mr. E. D. Smith, of Winona, who was a member of the last parliament and, I think, of some parliaments before that. I have his letter applying for compensation for the cases which he burnt last year. I felt a good deal of sympathy with Mr. Smith who, in this public-spirited way. destroyed these cases without hesitation. I have the invoices and statements and find that the loss from these importations came to $92. Of that, under this proposal we should pay about $60. When this application came in, Dr. Saunders, director of the experimental farm, wrote to the chief of the bureau of Horticulture of the State of New York, and found that under their old law they could not pay nursery men for cases, burned, but they found so many instances of hardship and such a movement in regard to the matter that they were amending their old law so as- to authorize the Commissioner of Agriculture to pay for such losses. I believe that the amendment has since been made. I am perfectly satisfied, from my experience both with the San Jose Scale Act and the Contagious Diseases of - Animals Act that we axe likely to secure the much more hearty co-operation of nurserymen and importers in our work by giving compensation. The small cost that is likely to be involved will be amply repaid by the greater willingness on the part of these people to give us information. My hon. friend (Mr. Goodeve) speaks of the effect of the commercial system. I dare say that works in some ways, but I am informed by those importers that, as a matter of
fact, they have to send the money before they gqt the goods. These are perishable goods, and the people who ship them, I suppose, do not want to run the risk of the voyage and handling. There may be cases where compensation can properly be given -I mean a general class of cases, not individual cases-and others, in which it would not be necessary or proper. It is for that reason that we take the power to do this by order in council. That order in council, of course, will not provide that John Jones shall get compensation, and Peter Smith shall not get it, but will declare what line of occurrences would call for the payment of compensation. I considered this matter very carefully before deciding to put it into the Bill, and, for the reasons I have given, I think it in the interests of the efficient carrying out of the Bill that we should have power, undeT certain circumstances, to pay compensation.

I can see why exporters should sometimes demand payment in advance. Fruit stock is perishable and the handling may easily cause loss. But, from my own experience of the commercial side extending over a good many years, I should think that if a man were importing from a house, doing business with them from time to time, and wrote back making a claim, pointing out that through their own fault the loss had occurred, he could secure payment for the damage. Where the fault was their own in sending diseased stock any reputable exporting firm would make an allowance. In the cases cited by the minister, where the importer voluntarily destroys cases, I agree that there should be compensation. But what I contend is that the general order allowing compensation would work along the lines I have indicated. If the importer has the government's own certificate that the stock has been destroyed because of disease, he has final evidence that his claim for compensation is just. I am not sure that an absolute legal claim could mot be made, though that would depend upon the conditions of the bargain. But, on general principles, I believe compensation could be had from the importer. 1 can see that granting government compensation might give rise to difficulties on the lines I have suggested.

It seems to me we are running great risk in allowing this to go on. A gentleman who had raised some of this stock, speaking to me a year or two ago, said that if it were not for the competition from European countries, we could create quite an industry in this country. But, owing to the cheapness of labour in Germany and France, they could produce this stock at very low rates and our nurserymen insisted on buying it there. I do mot see why we should run the risk of im-

porting any further tests into our country when we can produce this stock equally as good if not better at home. If something were done to encourage the nurserymen or to comnel them to raise in Canada the natural stock of the country we would not be taking any chances of importing the brown-tail moth or any other pest.
My hon. friend knows that there is a duty on these things which gives the home producer an advantage.
Not so much as the difference in labour.
It is twenty-five per cent, if I remember rightly.

I cannot heln but feel justified in taking the position that I have. It would be a good thing if this clause could be amended so that people in Canada would receive a payment of two-thirds of the value of that which was destroyed.
Nobody but Canadians would receive it.
Yes, the minister said that he would like to have the privilege of paying the Canadian for his potato crop.
Yes.

That is all right, but if we pay the foreigner two-thirds of what his goods cost, I think we are going a little beyond what we should do. I feel that we would be justified in amending this clause so that the foreigners sending his goods into this country would lose the boxes, and the packing, which would only amount to a few dollars in each case, but which would make him more careful.

I am afraid that the foreigners will not lose anything at all. The Canadian importer will have to pay the foreigner the full value, and he will not get anything back from him. He, and not the foreigner, will lose it. If the goods are destroyed in Canada in consequence of the existence of disease under this clause, the Canadian importer will lose the full value of them, and by this clause he may be compensated to the value of two-thirds.
He will be more careful.	.

This Bill gives the government the power that they never possessed before, not only of dealing with trees, and vegetables, and of entering upon any man's premises, but of destroying his crop, or orchard. This provision is followed by power to appoint inspectors, and by penalty clauses. While I am not personally familiar with the legislation in the various provinces, I know that Ontario is doing a very great deal of good work of this kind, and Mr. SEXSMITH.
that Nova Scotia is doing something. With Quebec horticultural methods I am not at all familiar, but I am thoroughly familiar with what we are doing in British Columbia. I recognize that it is in the interests of horticulture that if any province is not carrying on work of this kind, and if there are serious inroads being made by fungus diseases, and insect pests, it will be helpful to have power to do these very things; but where, as in British Columbia, we are doing these things with thoroughness and have a large body of officials, and knowing also, as I have reason to know, the difficulty in getting qualified men always to ascertain what is the real source of injury, the question arises as to the advisability of duplicating these services. When in 1898, 1899, and 1901, the province of Ontario appointed a large corps of inspectors under the San Jose Scale Act I do not suppose that there were half a dozen in the whole body who knew the difference between an armoured, and an unarmoured scale. There is the difficulty. If the minister should appoint a lot of inspectors to carry out this Act there may be the same natural difficulty from their want of technical knowledge. But where we have, as in British Columbia, a large body of inspectors, while we are anxious to co-operate with the Dominion, I think we want some reasonable assurance that this clause will not be put into effect in our case, as long as we are carrying on that work. I would like to see any possible clash of jurisdiction avoided.

I quite sympathize with my hon. friend. I tried to say this afternoon that where a properly constituted provincial authority is doing work of this kind, I should shrink from entering upon the field. I should only do so where I felt it was absolutely necessary in the interests of the whole country. As far as British Columbia is concerned I do not wish either to relieve the provincial government from the responsibility of this work, or to interfere with it. I would take great pains to see that we do not overlap where it can possibly be avoided. I take the words of the hon. gentleman as being almost authoritative,- because I know the influence that he would have with the British Columbia government, and I am quite sure that his influence would be in the direction of procuring thorough co-operation betweeen the officers, and authorities in British Columbia, and my own officers, and myself. I would welcome that not only from that province, but from all other provinces. I said to the hon. member for Digby (Mr. Jameson) that I knew what the provincial government of Nova Scotia were doing in connection with the brown-tail moth. If we can aid them in any way I shall see to it that we do so, but I shall not think of interfering with, or trying to override any

action that they have taken. I think, however, without absolute knowledge, that this Act gives a little greater authority than any of the provincial Acts do, except that of British Columbia, and that the machinery created, or to be created, by this Act, and the regulations under it will give me a little better facility for carrying out certain things than is in existence in any of the provinces, with the possible exception of British Columbia. The Ontario government has passed several Acts covering somewhat the same ground, but I do no't think any one of them is quite so complete, and I am not speaking with the idea of imputing any blame, or censure in the matter. I am simply speaking from having examined these Acts, while drawing this up, and I think perhaps this Act is a little more complete than theirs. From the fact that the regulations under this Act will apply to the whole country it gives a greater safeguard than could possibly accrue from the Act of any one province.

Did the minister consult the different local governments when he was preparing this Bill? There is a feeling in Canada that there is too muclj overlapping legislation between the Dominion and the provinces, and that a great deal of ex-' pense and much trouble would be saved if there was more concurrent action on matters of this kind.
We sent to Mr. C. C. James of the Department of Agriculture, Ontario, a copy of this Act, and communications have passed between us on the subject.
I commend the minister for that, and I trust that the -example will be followed in the future under similar circumstances.

I recognize the assistance such interchange of views lias always been to me in my departmental work.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Since this Bill has been introduced, the department has ascertained that the provision with regard to electrical units does not meet with the unanimous approval of the international committee, and it has been suggested that it should be deferred for another year. I move that the order be discharged.
What are the reasons?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I have stated them briefly. At the congress of electrical experts held in London, representing nearly all countries in the world using electricity, a sub-committee was appointed to prepare a description of electrical units which should be uniform throughout the world, and that description is contained in the Bill before the House. Later, the sub-committee disagreed in respect to one or two of the measures of electrical units and they have recommended that this Bill shall not be proceeded with until after a meeting which within a few months will be held in Washington. PUGSLEY moved second reading of Bill (No. 103) to amend the Navigable Waters Protection Act. He said: This Bill repeals sections 4 and 5 of the Navigable Waters Protection Act, chapter 115 of the Revised Statutes, and substitutes the following;
No bridge, boom, dam, aboiteau, wharf, dock, pier, or other structure of any kind, shall be built or placed in or across any navigable water, unless the site thereof has been approved by the Governor in Council, nor unless such bridge, boom, dam, aboiteau, wharf, dock, pier, or other structure is built and maintained in accordance with plans approved by the Governor in Council.
Section 5 is as follows:
Any work to which this part applies, which is built upon a site not approved by the Governor in Council, or which is not built in accordance with plans so approved, or which, having been so built, is not maintained in accordance with such plans, may be removed and destroyed under the authority of the Governor in Council.
I will read the sections of the present Act so that hon. gentlemen will see in what particulars the changes are made. Section 4 of chapter 115 is as follows:
No bridge, boom, dam or aboiteau shall be constructed so as to interfere with navigation, unless the site thereof has been approved of by the Governor in Council, nor unless such bridge, boom, dam or aboiteau is built and maintained in accordance with plans approved by the Governor in Council.

It will be seen that that is limited to bridge, boom, dam or aboiteau. It makes . no reference to a wharf, dock, pier or other structure. Then, strange to say, section 5 of the present Act simply reiers to a bridge. It says:
Any bridge to which this part applies, which is built upon a site not approved by the Governor in Council, or which is not built in accordance with plans so approved, or which, having been so built, is not maintained in accordance with such plans, in so far as the same interferes with navigation, may be lawfully removed and destroyed under the authority of the Governor in Council.
It will be seen that the object of this Bill is to give a larger measure of control to the Governor in Council over navigable waters. Section 4 of the present Act, while limited to a bridge, a boom, a dam, or an aboiteau, simply provides that it shall he constructed so as not to interfere with navigation. That leaves it doubtful as to what authority is to determine whether or not anv structure of this kind does interfere with navigation. I have had a number of cases brought to my attention where bridges have been erected across navigable waters. This has been so particularly in our western provinces, where, as -would naturally be the case in the early development of the country, there would not be steamers operating on the navigable rivers, or where, by reason of the necessity of certain improvements, navigation, while good in some parts, would not, on the whole, be suitable for the larger steamers; and some of the provincial governments have built bridges without coming to the Department of Public Works for approval. I have in mv mind a notable instance of a bridge being erected by a provincial government across the South Saskatchewan river. That was erected without any provision for navigation and evidently on the theory that as there was no navigation of the river by steamers at present, it could not be said that the bridge interfered with navigation.
Near what point is that?

Near Saskatoon, and a very unfortunate accident happened about two years ago. After the bridge was built, telegraph and telephone companies stretched wires across the river, which interfered with navigation to the same extent as the bridge; and a gentleman who owned a small vessel-I think he had built it further up the river-came down the river, and his vessel was caught in the wires and wrecked, and he sustained a loss of $11,000 or $12,000, for which he has not been able to obtain any redress. He could not obtain it from the Department of Public Works, because we had given no authority for the construction of the bridge or the Mr. PUGSLEY.
stringing of the telegraph or telephone wires across the river. It seems to me that in view of the great importance to this country of preserving navigation as far as possible, it is very desirable that there should be no works of any kind constructed in navigable waters without the plans being first submitted to the Department of Public Works, and approved by the minister and the Governor in Council. It is also rather extraordinary that section 4 of the Act at present makes no provision for wharfs, yet in most cases it has been recognized that the Department of Public Works has control over wharfs, and over and' over again we are asked to approve of the location of wharfs in navigable waters. This is, I think, as it should be. As the Dominion government is invested by the British North America Act with the control of navigation, it is most desirable, in the interests of the whole country, that when any person or company purposes to construct a work in a navigable water, that person or company should be compelled to come to the Department of Public Works and submit plans, and have those plans approved of before proceeding with the erection of the structure, whether it be a bridge, a wharf, a pier or any other structure that might interfere with navigation. I think the department and the Governor in Council ought to be the judge whether or not the work as proposed to be constructed would interfere with navigation or not. Of course, if it will not interfere with navigation it will be the duty of the department to grant its approval of the pronosed work. The Bill contains onlv the two sections which are to be in substitution of sections 4 and 5 of the present Act.

The hon. minister refers to docks and wharfs in addition to the structures mentioned in the old Act. I would like to ask him whether he '"s quite sure that in adding these words he will not interfere with private rights. The words are not confined to public docks or public wharfs, but refer to all wharfs and all docks. It may be difficult at times to know whether the property of a private individual alongside of a navigable water might or might not come under the Bill. If this parliament is undertaking to interfere with private property in that respect, it may be a somewhat serious question m some eases. The department might undertake to dictate to the owner of valuable property alongside of a navigable stream what he should or should not do with his own property. Does the hon. gentleman think that this government should control the property of individuals alongside such waters, if in its opinion the structures might interfere with navigation? If they were public

docks or wharfs which he intends to deal with, that might be another question, but the language of the Bill, as the hon. gentleman has explained it, would seem to cover everything in the nature of a dock or wharf adjoining navigable waters..

I do not see how we could properly safeguard navigation and make provision for the proper control over navigable waters unless we made the law general in its application. The present section provides that no bridge, dam or aboiteau shall be constructed so as to interfere with navigation. That gives the government control over work of that character, even although they might project from a shore belonging to a private individual. Of course the owner of a foreshore has no right to interfere with navigation because that is under control of the Dominion government, and therefore it is not unreasonable that before a private individual be allowed to build out into a navigable water a wharf or pier, he should come to the department and submit his plans. Let me give a case in point. A short time ago application was made to the department for approval of a wharf which the Grand Trunk Pacific proposed to construct in front of its property in the harbour of Victoria. That is just such a case as my hon. friend refers to.
That goes outside the Grand Trunk Pacific property as I understand it.

Not any more than if a private owner proposed to build a wharf out into a navigable stream, and that is the only case to which this Bill would apply. That is what the Grand Trunk Pacific proposed to do. That company recognized that if the department had no control, it ought to have. They therefore took their plans to the Public Works Department for approval. I directed that their application should .be referred to the resident engineer, and he conferred with the other wharf owners, more especially with the Canadian Pacific railway and the harbour association of Victoria, and I think also with members of the board of trade. The objection was taken that if this wharf were allowed to be built as the Grand Trunk Pacific proposed, it would narrow the harbour and make it exceedingly difficult for steamers coming to the Canadian Pacific railway wharf to be handled with safety. The resident engineer then recommended that the dimensions of the proposed wharf should be cut down somewhat. The Grand Trunk Pacific agreed to this, the Canadian Pacific railway was satisfied, and so was the innei harbour association of Victoria, and the wharf, instead of being an injury to navigation, will be an aid to it. I only mention this as an illustration of a case where it is very desirable in the public interest that a plan of that wharf to be constructed in front of the property, owned by a private individual or a company, should be submitted to the department. Take the case of an individual owning property abutting upon navigable water and alongside of whom there was another individual also owning property. Bach might propose to build a wharf out into the navigable water and the result might be a very serious interference with navigation; but if application had to be made to the department, our engineer would have to examine and report and the wharfs would *have to be so constructed as to be an advantage instead of a hindrance to navigation. I think, therefore, that if the Dominion government is to properly discharge the duty it owes the public in this connection under the British North America Act, it is necessary to have the law amended as proposed. No public difficulty would be created and no private injury would be done because we must assume that the department would be reasonable and only exercise its power to prevent navigation being injuriously affected.

The case to which the hon. minister has referred is not one of those to which I alluded. He refers to a case in which the Grand Trunk Pacific propose to extend a wharf into navigable waters, not building upon its own property solely, but going beyond that into the property of the Crown. That was not the case I was putting. I asked whether the language of the Bill would enable the government to dictate to the proprietor of land adjoining a stream and prevent him constructing a pier or wharf on his own property without the approval of the government.
If the structure were not to project into navigable water, this section of the Bill would not affect it because it says: 'Shall be built or placed in or across any navigable water'.

There are a great many crown patents which extend to navigable waters and where a person building a wharf will build it on the margin of a navigable stream. It would be an infringement on civil rights if the government should say to him: ' You must not build your wharf except under our approval, you must build a particular class of wharf, we propose to build a wharf along there, and you must build yours in accordance with that. If the government wish to interfere with civil rights, with the property of individuals, with the right of an individual to build a wharf or dock on -his

own property adjoining a navigable stream, almost in the stream, but on his own water line, however much that may be in the interests of the public, it seems to me such interference should not be allowed against rights already acquired without expropriation and compensation. I do not sav that the Bill goes that far, I merely call attention to the matter which I would like to have discussed before the Bill passes.

I think the words are such as will not raise this difficulty.
No bridge, boom, dam, &c., shall be built or placed in or across any navigable water.
If a man was building just upon the line *of the navigable water, he would not come [DOT]under the provisions of that section, but where he builds out into the navigable water, he would come within the section.

Is it not extremely difficult to determine in any navigable stream where the navigability begins? I take it that every drop of the St. Lawrence river is navigable water from bank to bank. No private ownership of the bed of a navigable river is recognized. Any ownership in the bed of a river is subject to the superior control of navigation, and it cannot be used however inconvenient it may be to the private owner, and. however much it may interfere with his private rights. The whole of the water is navigable, and I do not think it is wise to say that to a depth of perhaps three feet it is not navigable and at ten feet it is. You have to recog-1 nize that in any navigable harbour or stream every drop of water is navigable water, and all private rights are subject to the superior control of navigation. The argument of the hon. member for Hamilton strikes the harbour of North Sydney, where-we have a string of wharfs along the shore, and I realize this Bill will be putting people building wharfs along th4 water to inconvenience. However, I recognize that the bottom of that harbour is subject to navigation, and that private rights, as far .as these private rights can be exercised, must not interfere with the higher right of navigation.

On the Detroit river, for [DOT]example, there are most valuable properties where the freehold runs out into much more than two or three feet of water. There are properties at Windsor and Sandwich, and all along the river, where I fancy the owners would be very much surprised to hear they had no private rights although there were only two or three or even more feet of water. It is only that point I am guarding against. I think we must have a little regard to rights that have been acquired and perhaps enjoyed for a century.
When we get into committee, I will be very glad to receive any [DOT]suggestions as to amendments.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time.

Mr. TEMPLEMAN moved the second reading of Bill (No. 132) to amend the Gas Inspection Act. He said:	The only important amendment in this Bill is the taking power to test for the calorific quality of gas. Another amendment is to substitute the word ' district ' instead of ' city, town or 'place>' to conform with the districts of the Inland Revenue Department. Another amendment is to decrease the permissible limit of error in the testing of gas meters. At present the permissible limit of error is three per cent m favour of the producer and four per cent in favour of the consumer. That is being narrowed down to two per cent and three per cent, thus giving us better meters. The other amendments are merely substituting the word 1 district ' and repeahng_ the clause respecting inspection, which will hereafter be by regulation.

In Hamilton we have believed that there was no provision to protect the users of gas, that they could furnish us with any quality of gas, and that there was no provision whereby the city could have the gas tested.
Mr. BEATTIE, Every city has a proper protection for its gas supply, and it is tested for quality frequently. In London the gas is tested regularly.
Are you speaking of artificial gas?
Yes, that is artificial gas.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Under the present Gas Inspection Act all artificial gas is inspected as to its quality, and its illuminating power. One of the best inspectors we have in Canada is in Hamilton, and I have never heard any complaint from there as to the inspection of artificial gas. Natural gas is not inspected as regards its illuminating qualities as, under the law, it is not supposed to be used as an illuminant, although it is so used. It is inspected for the purpose of determining that it does not contain sulphuretted hydrogen, which is a deadly noxious gas. The gas Act now on the statute-book was passed long before natural gas was in use in Ontario, and it does not recognize the use of natural gas as an illuminant. Under this Bill, we seek authority to test natural gas for its heating power, which authority we do not now possess. I think it is a fact gas is less

and less used as an illuminant, unless it is used with mantles, and when it is used with mantles, the quality it requires to possess is heating rather than illuminating power, as the mantle is made incandescent by the calorific power of the gas, and it is this calorific power which should be the basis of the test of natural gas.

Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section l,

I desire to ask the Minister of Inland Revenue arr explanation with regard to certain matters. For instance, the law provides that there shall be no sulphuretted hydrogen or ammonia in gas. Then, the section here proposed provides that something must be added to the gas to give it an odour. 1 ask the minister to explain what authority he has for stating that sulphuretted hydrogen in gas is more deadly than ordinary gas itself or methane?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I did not say sulphuretted hydrogen is more deadly than other gas; I am not enough of a chemist to know that. But I said that under the law sulphuretted hydrogen was not allowed to form part of gas used as an illuminant. It does not appear in artificial gas anywhere in Canada that I am aware of.
The advantage of the presence of sulphuretted hydrogen in natural gas is that it gives the peculiar odour that enables people using it to detect a leak.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I do not know that it gives its peculiar odour to natural gas altogether. But I say that, under the law, it must not appear in gas used as an illuminant.
I am taking issue with the minister. That clause was put into the previous Act to prevent, so far as possible, the use of natural gas.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: No.
I happen to be a little acquainted with this matter. What I want to know is why there is an objection to sulphuretted hydrogen?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
My information is that sulphuretted hydrogen is a deadly poison. If used in illuminating gas, and there is any escape into the room, it is extremely dangerous. The object of the provision of the law which has been on the statute-book for thirty or forty years is to prohibit the use of gas characterized by this dangerous quality. That is entirely different from the department haying power to make an odorless gas odorous. I do not know * 180
that gas is made in Canada which is inodorous. I wmuld suppose that the object of making gas odorous is that you can smell it, because inodorous gas escaping into a room would be an extremely dangerous thing. It could not be detected. Death might result, but, as a matter of fact, I think all gas is odorous more or less. Mv deputy says that he has not been required to compel anv manufacturer to put anything into the gas to make it odorous.

Of course natural gas is inodorous. You cannot detect it when it
escapes.

What makes the gas odorous is the sulphuretted hydrogen, and that sulphuretted hydrogen is not a particle more deadly than the natural gas itself. It does not form a new combination different from that which already exists?
How is it put in?

It comes there naturally. It is born in the gas the same as sulphur is in petroleum. There is a certain amount of sulphur in petroleum. There is a certain amount of sulphur in natural gas which is merely a higher fraction than petroleum. This provision was inserted in the Bill a number of years ago to prevent the people from using natural gas. Some artificial gas makei'3 said that natural gas was dangerous, and for that reason they compelled the producers of natural gas, when the gas was to be used for illuminating purposes, to put it through a process. I cannot understand why if natural gas is deadly when it escapes into a room, it is any more deadly than sulphuretted hydrogen.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I do not know enough about the peculiar properties of gases to debate the question with my hon. friend. My understanding is that if sulphuretted hydrogen in artificial or natural gas escapes into a room or is burned in a room it is an extremely dangerous thing; in fact, fatal. There is not a particle of sulphuretted hydrogen permitted in any artificial gas made in Canada. If one of our inspectors found its presence there he would immediately notify the manufactur-ers^and a change would be made, or the manufacturers would be fined if they allowed such gas to go into consumption. It is a fact that in many natural gases sulphuretted hydrogen is present. As a matter of fact, some of the wells had to be closed down because of it. We do not recognize the use of natural gas as an ii-luminant. There has been a continuous contest between the department, and some of the owners of wells in western Ontario, but we have not recognized it. The owners of wells do not undertake to sell thej.r gas as an illuminant. They sell it



for heating purposes, and the parties who buy the gas light their houses with it. Recently we have been endeavouring to get the owners of some of the gas wells, particularly around the city of Chatham, to use a small purifier, which I think is working satisfactorily. I have not caught the point of my hon. friend. We do not permit sulphuretted hydrogen in gas. The law has not permitted it before, and it is not proposed to permit it now. My hon. friend says that this is put in the Act for the purpose of preventing the use of natural ga3.
I do not think that is so. My deputy assures me it is not so. The Act. i3 older than the use of natural gas as an illum-inant, which is of recent date. Therefore, it could not have been put in for that purpose. The amendments that we are making now are for the purpose of still further strengthening the Act. We are going to take power and that is the principal amendment-to test the heating, or calorific power, of all gases. As gas is coming into universal use for heating purposes, and as it is disappearing as fin illuminant it is very necessary that we should have that power. It is not absolutely disapnearing as an illuminant, but where it is still used it is used with a mantle, and you very seldom see an open flame now. Where the mantle is used it is the calorific poorer, and not the illuminating power that is important, because heat has to be produced to make the mantle incandescent.

The original idea of preventing sulphuretted hydrogen in gas was to prevent gas makers from selling water gas. Now the world is going largely into the manufacture of water gas, and producers are able to sell Mond gas at a very low figure, and it will continue to be sold as heating gas. I do not think that this sulphuretted hydrogen, which is contained in the gas is any more deadly than the gas itself, any more than fusil oil is more., deadly than whisky. Either one will kill a man if he takes enough. I cannot understand why this clause is put into the Canadian Act, except to compel the sellers of natural gas to put the gas through an expensive cleaning process. You have to use iron filings to take the sulphur out of it, and it must go through a purifier. This gas is just as safe as the gas that is used in a gas engine. The producer gas used in a gas engine has that sulphuretted hydrogen in it, and if you are going to have it taken out of illuminating gas you might as well say that a factory should have it taken out of the gas that it uses for industrial purposes. With what little knowledge I have of the practical use of gas in engines and of the use of natural gas, I am led to the conclusion that this is a fool provision. It is a fool provision that was put into the Act away back fifty years ago, and is still held on to.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: What does my hon. friend want changed?

The objection-1 have to this Bill is the provision in paragraph ;(d) of section 31. We have not reached that yet, but you are dealing with it in clause (b) of the first section. 'You compel them to take the nasty smell out of the gas by clause 31 by removing sulphuretted hydrogen, and m clause 3 you compel them to put something else in the gas to give it a smell.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Subsection 3 has -been the law for many years, and I am advised that none of the gas made in Canada is inodorous, and every one knows that inodorous gas would be very dangerous if it leaked. In subsection 3 we have added ' for testing the calorific power of gas,' which is a very necessary provision. There is no inspection now for testing the calorific power of gas, and it is coming into general use for heating purposes.
Do you fix a standard?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: We will fix a standard by regulation.
You have power to test and inspect in the Act, but so far as I see, you have no power to fix a standard.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I have no objection to add the words ' for testing the calorific power of gas and establishing standards therefor.'

That is right.
Clause, -as amended, agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: In subclause (d), I add a new section: ' for testing the illuminating power of gas,' and to that I will add the words suggested by the hon. member (Mr. J. A. Currie), ' and establishing standards therefor.' Then, in subsection (e), to the words 'or testing the purity of gas,' we will also add the words ' and establishing standards therefor.'

That appears to be all right.
On section 3, meters to comply with true standard measure.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
This is one of the important amendments. It limits the percentage of errors in the meter. The old law allowed 3 per cent in favour of the seller and 4 per cent in favour of the consumer. We are now narrowing the limit down to 2 per cent and 3 per cent, respectively, thus making the meter more perfect.
On section 4, undertaking of gas makers as to supply and quality of gas.

The complaint is made that sometimes natural gas is supplied at far too great a pressure. Has the minister taken into consideration an amendment to provide that it shall not be delivered to the consumer above a certain pressure?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I am advised that gas from a natural well could not be taken into a house at the natural pressure of the well, and that as a matter ot fact it is always reduced to a very small pressure.
Sometimes it is not reduced enough, and, therefore, causes leaks in the joints of the pipes, which in turn cause explosions in houses.

I would suggest that the minister use the words, ' proper and sufficient pressure.'
Amendment as proposed agreed to.

I have already taken exception to paragraph (d), which says that the gas 'shall exhibit no trace of sulphuretted hydrogen or any excess of sulphur and ammonia.' I think the department has sufficient power to make regulations without the necessity of a statutory enactment of this kind, and, moreover, this is not necessary, because I do not think that it can be shown that sulphuretted hydrogen is poisonous.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: This clause is regarded by the department as most important. The very reason why we inspect gas is that no trace of sulphuretted hydrogen is permitted in it. These provisions, I am advised by the experts of the department, are essential to the proper inspection of gas. Its nurity and its illuminating quality are the two great points. My hon. friend says that we can make regulations covering these provisions. If so, there can be no objection to having them in the Act.
I say that neither the hon. gentleman nor any chemist can show me that sulphuretted hydrogen is poisonous.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I am advised that no chemist in the world will agree with my hon. friend. A year ago, when we tried to legalize the use ,of natural gas as an illuminant, the chemist of our department would not permit natural gas, with 1 per cent of sulphuretted hydrogen in it, to be used as an illuminant.

I take issue with the chemist of the denartment. I say that sulphuretted hydrogen is neither nois-onous nor does it form an element in the compound when burned. It happens to be a component of two very cheap gases which the public want to use: one is nat-i8oa
ural gas, and the other is Mond gas; and this clause is kept in the Act to compel these gases to be put through very expensive processes in order to remove the smell of sulphuretted hydrogen, which is not dangerous and thereby to make the gas more expensive to the consumer. I say again that, from my knowledge of chemistry, which is not very great and should not be any greater than the minister's, who is a doctor, sulphuretted hv-drogen is not poison, and I do not think he can find anybody who can show that it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I am not a chemist but nothing has been impressed upon me so much in the administration of this Act by the experts of the department as the fact that sulphuretted hydrogen is poisonous. The chief inspector gives me this memo:
Sulphuretted hydrogen is the one poison in gas which is not destroyed by combustion, but escapes into the room as sulphurous acid gas. The other poisonous constituents are destroyed by combustion.
The whole inspection of manufactured gas in Canada during all these years has been with the view of eliminating the very-last particle of sulphuretted hydrogen.

An ordinary coal stove will produce more sulphuretted hydrogen in a room than half a dozen gas jets, there is no question but that it is an expensive process to take the sulphuretted hydrogen out of natural gas, more especially out of the cheaper gas called Mond gas. The regulations are already sufficient. Clause 3 permits the department to 'take steps to protect the public so that it is not necessary to have clause 4. If at any time the department wishes to relax their regulations they can do so, but under this clause they cannot.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
In accordance with the hon. gentleman's suggestion, I wpuld move that after the words ' by regulation made by the minister,' in the fourth line, the words ' or not in accordance with the standard ' be substituted.
Section, as amended, agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I also desire to add the general penalty clause which we have in all our Inland iRevenue Acts as subsection 3 of section 8:
Every person who violates any of the provisions of this Act, or any of the regulations established under this Act, or who neglects any duty imposed on him by this Act, or by any such regulation for which violation or neglect no penalty is specially herein provided, shall incur a penalty of not less than $25 and not more than $100.
Subsection, as amended, agreed to.

speechtext:
